PSX Tracker guide

Export and reconcile your PSX portfolio

A tracker earns trust only when it matches reality. Export on a schedule and reconcile after big imports, rights issues or messy scan days. This article is a practical checklist.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

What to export and keep

Use in-app export or Sheets-related flows when available so you have a dated copy outside the browser. Store it where you can find last month’s file.

Exports complement Drive sync; they are snapshots you can email to an advisor or diff locally.

Reconcile holdings

Compare quantity and average cost per ticker with the broker app. Investigate mismatches before the next sell so FIFO lots stay clean.

Common culprits: duplicate imports, wrong symbols, forgotten corporate actions, or trades entered in the wrong portfolio.

Reconcile cash and income

Check deposits, withdrawals and dividends against bank or broker cash reports for overlapping dates.

If withholding appears on dividends, ensure your ledger’s net and tax lines can explain the credit you saw.

After you fix the book

Correct trades, export again, and sync Drive so every device shares the cleaned state. Then place new trades.

Reconciliation is boring — and cheaper than rebuilding a year of lots in April.

This guide is educational and describes how PSX Tracker works. It is not investment, tax or legal advice. Confirm rules and figures with your broker, FBR guidance and professional advisors.

Why export if the screen already looks right

The screen is a view. The export is a file you can diff against a statement without the app in the way. It is also the copy that survives a login problem, a phone replacement, or a restore you regret. Export on a schedule, name the file with the date, and store it next to the broker PDF for the same date.

Reconcile means proving that three things match: quantities, cash, and the corporate actions you were party to. A match on quantity with a wrong cost is only a partial match. You will feel it later, when a sale’s gain looks nothing like the contract note.

Do the work when you are not in a hurry to file or to pay someone. A calm hour finds the duplicated import. A panicked hour “fixes” it with an adjusting entry you will not understand in June.

Quantities first

For each symbol, write the broker or CDC quantity and the tracker quantity. Differences come from a missing buy, a duplicated sell, a bonus you did not record, or a transfer between portfolios that only one side received. Fix the event. Do not type a dummy trade at a made-up price to force the number.

Funds get the same treatment against the asset-manager statement. Units, not rupees, are the first check. Rupees move every time NAV moves. Units move only when you transact or when the fund issues a corporate action.

If a symbol exists in the tracker and not at the broker, you may have typed a buy that never filled, or you may be looking at the wrong broker’s login. The broker field on the trade is the clue.

Cash second

List deposits, withdrawals, buys, sells, dividends, and fees. Buys spend cash. Sells add cash only for the quantity you actually held. A sell of shares you did not own should not increase cash, because the proceeds were not yours. Dividends add the net cash and record the tax separately. Transfers of shares between your own books do not move cash at all.

A negative cash balance is a signal, not a mood. It means the cash events you recorded cannot fund the purchases you recorded. The usual causes are a missing deposit, a buy entered twice, a dividend never entered, or a transfer treated as a withdrawal. Find which one. The identity is boring and reliable: if the events are complete, cash stops being a mystery.

Broker cash and bank cash are different. Do not expect the tracker’s broker cash to equal your bank account. Expect it to equal the broker’s client-wallet statement.

Costs and corporate actions third

Pick five trades, including one old and one recent, and match price, quantity, and fees to the contract notes. Fees are where silent drift lives. A missing commission on every buy makes you look richer than you are.

Then walk the year’s announcements for names you held: dividends, bonuses, rights, splits, face-value changes. Tick each one as recorded or as not applicable because you bought later. Face value matters when a dividend is declared as a percentage. A change in face value that you ignore will scale that dividend wrong.

Average cost on the broker screen and FIFO cost in the tracker are allowed to disagree. They are different questions. Reconcile both to the lots, not to each other. The FIFO guide shows a small numerical example of that disagreement.

Close the loop

When quantities, cash, and the sample of contract notes match, write the date on the export. That file is a known-good point. A later import can be compared with it. If the later import is wrong, restore to the known-good file instead of editing blindly. Keep at least two of those dated files. A single export that you overwrite every Sunday is not a history.

If they do not match and you cannot see why, stop adding trades. Export the broken book anyway, so you have it, and ask for help with a specific symbol and date. Support can think about a missing lot. Support cannot think about “it’s all off.” A named symbol, a date, and the two quantities is enough to start.

Reconciliation is the product working. The dashboard is just the dashboard. Trust it after the statement agrees, and not before.

Common questions

Why export if the app already shows the book?

An export lets you compare holdings, cash, and dividends with a broker or CDC statement line by line.

What should I check after an import?

Quantities, average cost, cash, and dividends, especially after a bonus, split, or a scan that you edited.

Which file is authoritative?

Your broker, CDC, and fund statements. The tracker is your working copy of what you entered.
